content.description: On Christmas Day 800, in Rome, Pope Leo III placed a crown on Charlemagne's head. The West had an emperor again, and Europe had a model that would last.

hero.hook: Christmas 800: a Frankish king becomes emperor, and Europe enters a new age.

blocks.text: On **December 25, 800**, in St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, Pope **Leo III** placed a crown on the head of **Charles**, king of the Franks. The gesture claimed to restore the Roman Empire, gone from the West since **476**.

This was more than a ceremony. It was the birth of an ambition: a Latin Christian empire, separate from Byzantium (the Eastern Roman Empire), which laid the administrative and cultural foundations of continental Europe.

**Charlemagne** inherited the Frankish kingdom in **768**. After his brother's death, he conquered without pause. Thirty years of war against the **Saxons**, Germanic peoples of what is now Germany, forced conversion included. In **774**, he brought down the [[Lombard]] kingdom of northern Italy. He subdued Bavaria, crushed the [[Avars]], nomadic horsemen of the Danube, and pushed into Spain, where the ambush at [[Roncevaux Pass]] in **778**, high in the Pyrenees, passed into legend.
At its peak, the empire covered about **1.1 million km²**. That was far too vast to hold by the sword alone. Charles had to invent another way to govern.
Charlemagne stood about **1.84 m** tall, remarkable at a time when the average man was closer to **1.65 m**.

To hold the empire together, Charlemagne relied on [[Counts]], who governed locally, and on [[The missi dominici]], inspectors sent out in pairs to keep watch over the provinces. In Aachen, his capital, [[Alcuin of York]], an English scholar, ran the palace school. Latin was restored, clerics were trained, and a new script was invented, **Carolingian minuscule**, legible everywhere.

Monasteries copied the texts of antiquity. On the economic side, the [[Silver denarius]] replaced gold, which had grown too scarce: a stable coin for everyday trade. This was the **Carolingian Renaissance**, less a burst of artistic splendor than a victory for order and useful knowledge.
So that his laws would be understood, Charlemagne insisted that they be read aloud to the people, on market days or after Mass.

sections.title: Governing and teaching people to read

blocks.text: In **799**, Leo III was attacked in Rome and took refuge with Charles, who put him back in power. On Christmas Day, the pope crowned him **“Emperor of the Romans.”** According to his biographer Einhard, Charles was uneasy about it: by placing the crown himself, the pope suggested that power came from the Church.

In Constantinople, the capital of Byzantium, this was denounced as usurpation. For the Byzantines there could be only one Roman emperor. Charlemagne created a second center of power. The Latin West asserted its independence, and out of that came the idea of [[The Holy Roman Empire]], which would last for centuries.

events.title: Treaty of Verdun

blocks.text: After **814**, the unity did not hold. In **843**, the Treaty of Verdun split the empire among Charlemagne's grandsons: France in the west, Germany in the east, and a contested strip in between. Local lords gained ground. But the counties, the script, the coinage and the imperial dream all survived.
The imperial title would last until **1806**. Charlemagne became the “Father of Europe,” not because his empire held together, but because he gave the West its first great common framework.

On **December 25, 800**, Charlemagne restored the Empire in the West. Broken up as early as **843**, the project still left Europe its first tools of unity: administration, writing, coinage and the imperial idea.

content.title: What changed when Charlemagne was crowned on Christmas 800?

Alcuin of York.explanation: English scholar brought in by Charlemagne to lead the Palatine School in Aachen. He oversaw the reform of writing and education, training a generation of literate administrators who maintained the empire.

Avars.explanation: Nomadic horse-riding people originally from Central Asia, settled in the Danube plain, whose empire was destroyed by Carolingian armies.

Count.explanation: High local dignitary appointed by the sovereign to administer a province (the county) in his name, holding military and judicial powers.

Counts.explanation: High local dignitaries appointed by the sovereign to administer a province (the county) in his name, possessing military and judicial powers.

Holy Roman Empire.explanation: Politics entity born from The Coronation of Charlemagne (800), claiming to embody the continuity of the Roman Empire in the West under Christian authority. It lasted until 1806 and structured the Germanic space for a thousand years.

Lombard.explanation: Germanic people established in Northern Italy from the 6th century onwards, whose kingdom was conquered by Charlemagne in 774.

Roncevaux Pass.explanation: Pyrenean pass where the rear-guard of Charlemagne's army was massacred in 778 by the Vascons, an event which inspired the famous 'Song of Roland'.

Silver denarius.explanation: Reference currency imposed by Charlemagne's monetary reform, replacing gold with silver as the basis of the European economic system for several centuries.

The Holy Roman Empire.explanation: Politics entity born from The Coronation of Charlemagne (800), claiming to embody the continuity of the Roman Empire in the West under Christian authority. It lasted until 1806 and structured the Germanic space for a thousand years.

The missi dominici.explanation: Carolingian "envoys of the master": royal inspectors sent in pairs (one bishop, one layman) to control local administration and render justice in the name of the emperor. Key instrument of Carolingian government over an immense territory.
